Sex-specific white matter alterations in children exposed to
high pregestational BMI

Abstract
Objective: This study investigated whether exposure to high pregestational BMI
(≥ 25 kg/m2
) is associated with alterations in white matter microstructure in early
childhood, explored sex-specific effects, and examined associations with cognitive
performance.
Methods: A total of 90 children from the Alberta Pregnancy Outcomes and Nutrition
(APrON) cohort underwent diffusion tensor imaging between ages 2 and 7 years.
Data were processed using ExploreDTI to obtain mean fractional anisotropy (FA) and
mean diffusivity (MD). Pregestational weight was self-reported by pregnant individuals, height was measured at enrollment, and child cognitive outcomes were assessed
at ages 3 to 4 years using the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence.
Results: Children exposed to high pregestational BMI had lower FA, but not higher
MD, in the superior longitudinal fasciculus and in the body and splenium of the corpus callosum compared with unexposed children (BMI 18.5–24.9 kg/m2
). This association persisted when analyzing pregestational obesity and overweight categories

separately. Altered FA in splenium of the corpus callosum was associated with poorer
cognitive outcomes in exposed children. Exposed male children had higher FA in the
fornix, whereas female children had lower FA in the body and splenium of the corpus
callosum compared with unexposed peers.
Conclusions: High pregestational BMI was associated with alterations in white matter microstructure during early childhood in a sex-specific manner. Promoting healthy
lifestyles and weight management among individuals of childbearing age is crucial.
INTRODUCTION
Globally, the prevalence of high body weight is rising significantly,
raising substantial public health concerns. Among individuals of childbearing age, the prevalence of high body weight has increased significantly over the past decades, with 25% of Canadian individuals ages
18 to 34 years classified as living with obesity (body mass index
[BMI] ≥ 30 kg/m2
) and 28% classified as having overweight (BMI ≥ 25
and <30 kg/m2
) [1]. High body weight before or during pregnancy is
associated with complications such as gestational diabetes [2]. These
complications can persist beyond pregnancy, potentially influencing
birth outcomes that include prematurity and congenital anomalies and
increasing the risk of adiposity, neurodevelopmental impairments such
as poor cognitive performance, and neurodevelopmental disorders

such as attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder [3, 4]. These findings
suggest a potential negative relationship between fetal exposure to
high body weight and neurodevelopment in children, although the
underlying mechanisms for these associations are still not well understood. Toward that end, identifying neural markers of exposure to

high pregestational BMI is crucial for understanding how high body
weight might relate to brain development. Such markers could enable
health professionals to screen children who are born at risk and provide opportunities for early intervention.
Exposure to various intrauterine factors (e.g., alcohol) can
affect brain development, particularly white matter microstructure
(for detailed review, see Lebel and Deoni [5]). In general, most
white matter tracts are present by term gestation (37–41 weeks),
but the process of myelination continues into late childhood and
adulthood [5]. Given the prolonged maturation of white matter,
any disturbances owing to prenatal exposures could have a cascading effect on subsequent development [6]. Diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) is a useful neuroimaging technique that allows for the
characterization of water diffusion properties in the brain, particularly within white matter tracts, which are highly sensitive to these
diffusion properties [7].
Animal models have shown associations between high maternal body weight before and during pregnancy and altered brain
development in offspring [8–10]. However, in humans, only four
DTI studies, to our knowledge, have examined white matter development in offspring exposed to high pregestational BMI [11–14],
with most focusing on the neonatal period [11–13]. These studies
have identified lower fractional anisotropy (FA) in widespread
white matter tracts, including association, projection, callosal, and
limbic fibers, among neonates exposed to high pregestational BMI
compared with those born to people with normal-weight pregestational BMI (18.5–24.9 kg/m2
). Interestingly, one study found an
association between pregestational BMI and higher FA in multiple
white matter tracts, including association and projection fibers, in
offspring ages 10 to 26 years, but not at age 6 years [14]. Collectively, these studies have reported mixed results across different
developmental stages. Therefore, further research is warranted
with an additional focus on different levels of pregestational BMI.
To date, no studies, to our knowledge, have investigated the relationship between high pregestational BMI and white matter development in offspring during early childhood, a period of rapid

myelination [15, 16], or have examined the association with neurodevelopmental outcomes.
We investigated major white matter tracts in early childhood
among children born to people with high pregestational BMI compared with those born to people with normal-weight pregestational
BMI. Guided by earlier observations in this study cohort [17], we also
examined whether altered white matter tracts were associated with
poorer cognitive performance in children born to people with high
pregestational BMI. Our a priori hypothesis was that exposure to
high pregestational BMI would be associated with lower FA in the
white matter microstructure of offspring during early childhood and
that these alterations would be associated with cognitive
performance. Given that white matter development can be influenced
by factors such as length of gestation, sex, and exposure to other metabolic conditions (e.g., diabetes) and toxic substances, we also
explored the effect of these factors on our findings through subgroup
and sensitivity analyses.
METHODS
Study design and participants
The Alberta Pregnancy Outcomes and Nutrition (APrON) study is a
prospective longitudinal study of pregnant women and their children
in the central and southern regions of Alberta, Canada. Originally, it
aimed to explore the relationships among nutrition, mental health, and
neurodevelopment [18].
A subset of children between ages 2 and 7 years from the APrON
study was eligible for brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) if they
were born at or after 35 weeks’ gestation, spoke English as their primary language, had no contraindications to MRI, and had no history of
neurodevelopmental disorders or neurological problems. All eligible
children were invited to participate, and those whose parents
Study Importance
What is already known?
• Exposure to high pregestational BMI can affect white
matter development in children, although findings have
been inconsistent.
• High pregestational BMI is associated with negative neurodevelopmental outcomes, but the underlying neural
mechanisms remain unclear.
What does this study add?
• This study demonstrates that exposure to high pregestational BMI is associated with alterations in specific white
matter tracts during early childhood, with distinct effects
on male and female children.
• Alterations in white matter development in these children
are associated with poorer cognitive outcomes.
How might these results change the direction of

research or the focus of clinical practice?
• These results emphasize the need for preconception
guidance and lifestyle interventions to improve health
and potentially reduce risks to fetal brain development.
• These results also encourage clinicians to consider longterm outcomes, allocate resources effectively, and closely
monitor children who may be at risk.

children completed the scan, resulting in a final sample of 107 children
(Figure 1).
The APrON study was approved by the Conjoint Health Research
Ethics Board at the University of Calgary. Written informed consent
was obtained from the parent/guardian, and verbal assent was

assessment, and questionnaire completion.
MRI data acquisition
Children underwent brain MRI scans using a research-dedicated GE
Discovery MR750w 3.0-T scanner (GE HealthCare) with a 32-channel
head coil at Alberta Children’s Hospital in Calgary, Canada. In order to
prepare children for MRI scanning, families received reading materials
and were offered one or more practice sessions in an MRI simulator.
During the scan, children watched a video of their choice, wore soft
silicone earplugs, and had padding around their heads to help them
stay still. DTI was acquired with the following parameters: b = 750 s/
mm2
; 30 gradient directions; repetition time (TR) = 6750 ms; echo
time (TE) = 79 ms; and voxel size = 1.6  1.6  2.2 mm (resampled
on scanner to 0.78  0.78  2.2 mm). Five interleaved images without diffusion encoding (b = 0 s/mm2
) were acquired. The entire DTI
acquisition took 5 min.
Diffusion data processing

All diffusion images were visually inspected for quality, and volumes
with excessive artifacts or motion corruption were removed (Figure 1;
for details, see Reynolds et al. [19]). The diffusion data were processed using ExploreDTI (version 4.8.6), with corrections for signal
drift, Gibbs ringing, participant motion, and eddy current distortion.
Semiautomated deterministic streamline tractography was used
to delineate the following 11 major white matter tracts: the pyramidal
tract; corpus callosum (genu, body, and splenium); cingulum; fornix;
inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus; inferior longitudinal fasciculus;
superior longitudinal fasciculus; arcuate fasciculus; and uncinate
fasciculus. Detailed processing methods have been described elsewhere [19]. Briefly, the most representative scan (from a 3.68-yearold female) was identified using tract-based spatial statistics. Regions
of interest (ROIs) were drawn on this target scan. The semiautomated
tractography method ensured that ROIs were consistently placed
across all children’s scans by normalizing each scan to the target and
applying inverse transformations to warp the ROIs back to native
space. The delineated tracts were manually inspected, and spurious
fibers were removed as necessary.
Average FA and mean diffusivity (MD) were extracted for each
tract in each child. Except for the corpus callosum and fornix, values
were calculated separately for left and right hemisphere tracts and
subsequently averaged. Previous research by Kar et al., using the
same subset of children, found little evidence of asymmetry in FA and
MD of these tracts [20].
Exposure
Pregestational weight (kilograms) was obtained from self-reported
data provided by pregnant individuals at the time of recruitment (first
or second trimester of pregnancy). Previous studies have demonstrated that these self-reports are valid measures of actual pregestational weight [21]. Height (meters) was measured three times during
the visit, and the average of these measurement was used. Pregestational BMI was then calculated using the following formula: weight in
kilograms divided by height in meters squared. For analysis purposes,
pregestational BMI was classified according to the World Health

Organization standards as follows: normal weight (18.5–24.9 kg/m2
,
reference); overweight (25.0–29.9 kg/m2
); and obesity (≥30.0 kg/m2).
Children born to people classified as having underweight (<18.5 kg/
m2
) were excluded from the present study (Figure 1).
Neuropsychological testing
Children underwent neuropsychological testing administered by a
trained psychometrician at ages 3 to 4 years (range 3.1–4.9 years).
Full-scale intelligence (FSIQ) was assessed using the Wechsler Preschool and Primary Scale of Intelligence, 4th Edition, Canadian
(WPPSI-IVCND) [22]. The WPPSI-IVCND measures intelligence in children between age 2 years and 6 months and age 7 years and 7 months
and has demonstrated a reliability coefficient (Cronbach α) greater
than 0.9 [23]. In addition to the FSIQ, we examined the following
three primary indices from the WPPSI-IVCND: verbal comprehension
(VCI); visual spatial (VSI); and working memory (WMI). These indices
are composite scores derived from specific subtests of the WPPSIIVCND, which together make up the FSIQ. All of these scores were
age-standardized (mean [SD], 100 [15]).
Confounders/covariates
The following variables were selected based on their known association with pregestational BMI and/or white matter development:
age of the child at the time of MRI; sex of the child; gestational age
at birth; birth weight z score; socioeconomic status (based on
household income and education); and maternal age at the time of
delivery. Gestational age and birth weight are highly correlated;
therefore, birth weight was converted to a z score adjusted for
gestational age and sex, based on Canadian birth reference
standards.
Smoking or alcohol consumption during pregnancy were not considered owing to the small number of cases (Table 1).
Participants completed questionnaires during the first study visit
(i.e., first or second trimester) that captured information regarding
sociodemographic variables (i.e., household income and education)

and pregnancy-related variables (i.e., age at the time of delivery,
tobacco/alcohol use during pregnancy, diabetes during or before
pregnancy, and hypertension during or before pregnancy). Moreover,
the incidence of gestational hypertension and gestational diabetes
was obtained from birth records. In order to ensure accuracy, maternal health conditions, including gestational hypertension and gestational diabetes, were cross-checked with electronic medical records.
Women recruited to the APrON study provided their Alberta Health

personal health number and consented to access of their health
records during pregnancy and delivery.
Information on neonatal outcomes (i.e., sex, birth weight, and gestational age) was retrieved from medical records.
Statistical analysis
Cohort characteristics were assessed using standard descriptive statistics (number, percentage, and mean [standard deviation, SD]). Student
t test or Pearson χ 2 test was used, as appropriate, to compare characteristics of children and pregnant individuals between high pregestational BMI (≥25.0 kg/m2
) and normal-weight pregestational BMI
(18.5–24.9 kg/m2
) groups.
The prespecified primary outcome was FA of white matter tracts,
whereas the secondary outcome was MD of white matter tracts.
For the primary analysis, we compared FA between children born
to people with high pregestational BMI and those with normal-weight
pregestational BMI using multiple linear regression, with the normalweight pregestational group as the reference. The outcome variable

was FA, and the exposure variable was pregestational BMI, categorized as binary with two levels (i.e., high vs. normal weight). We estimated unstandardized regression coefficients (B) and standard errors
(SE) to reflect adjusted differences in FA, controlling for child age, sex,
gestational age at birth, birth weight z score, socioeconomic status
(based on household income and education), and age at time of
delivery.
A power analysis was conducted to ensure sufficient sample size
to detect meaningful between-group differences. With 90 children
(41.1% in exposed group) and assuming a large effect size (Cohen
d = 0.8) with a significance level of 0.05, the study achieved 92.4%
power to detect differences among BMI groups. Sensitivity analyses

were conducted separately, excluding children born preterm
(<37 weeks), those exposed to diabetes during pregnancy, and those
exposed to alcohol during pregnancy, plus a combined analysis excluding all three groups. In order to avoid overadjusting for potential mediators, we conducted additional sensitivity analyses excluding
gestational age and birth weight z score from the model.
In order to explore the effect of sex, we performed sex-stratified
analyses for male and female children as subgroup analyses.
For the secondary analysis, we used a similar approach to compare MD of white matter tracts between children born to people
with high pregestational BMI and those with normal-weight
pregestational BMI.
We further examined differences in FA across pregestational BMI
categories, particularly comparing those classified as having obesity,
overweight, and normal-weight BMI values. Using multiple linear
regression, we estimated B and SE, with FA as the outcome variable
and pregestational BMI categorized into three levels (i.e., obesity,
overweight, and normal weight), adjusting for the same covariates.
We also assessed FA differences between children born to people
with pregestational BMI classified as obesity versus overweight, again
using multiple linear regression with FA as the outcome variable and
pregestational BMI categorized into two levels (i.e., obesity and overweight), adjusting for the same covariates.
As part of our exploratory analysis, we investigated the association between FA and cognitive outcomes using multiple linear regression, treating cognitive outcomes as a continuous variable. FA was the
primary independent variable, alongside the following covariates: high
pregestational BMI category (≥25.0 kg/m2
; yes/no); age of the child;
sex of the child; gestational age; birth weight z score; maternal age at
time of delivery; and socioeconomic status, all across the entire
cohort. For significant findings, we conducted subgroup analyses comparing children born to people with high pregestational BMI and those
born to people with normal-weight BMI. This approach aimed to
determine whether the direction of the association was consistent
with that observed in the entire cohort. We included an interaction
term to assess whether the relationship between FA and cognitive

outcomes varied by pregestational BMI category (yes/no). Some children had missing data in their neuropsychological assessments, leading to their exclusion from the analysis. Baseline characteristics were
compared between included and excluded children using Student
t test or Pearson χ 2 test, as appropriate, to ensure the robustness of
our findings.
Detailed model specifications are provided in the online Supporting Information Methods.
We did not apply multiple comparison adjustments to the primary
analysis due to the exploratory nature of the study and the limited
research on white matter development in children exposed to high
pregestational BMI, which may help avoid overlooking meaningful
findings. A two-tailed p value threshold of <0.05 was used for statistical significance. For subgroup and secondary analyses, we applied
false discovery rate corrections separately for p values related to sex
and comparisons of BMI categories: obesity versus normal weight;
overweight versus normal weight; and obesity versus overweight.
Given our focus on the clinical significance of lower FA in specific
white matter tracts, we did not adjust associations between FA and
neuropsychological outcomes for multiple comparisons.
All analyses were conducted using R version 3.5 (RStudio IDE).
RESULTS
Participants
A total of 90 children were included in the DTI analysis (Table 1;
Figure 1). Of these, 41.1% were born to people with pregestational
BMI classified as obesity or overweight, with a mean maternal age of
32.1 years at delivery. Over one-half of the families reported a household income of CAD $100,000 or greater, 60% of the participants had
completed a university degree or higher, and fewer than 10% experienced pregnancy-related complications.
The mean age of the children at the time of MRI scanning was 3.6
(SD 0.9) years, with 52.2% being male. The mean gestational age at
birth was 39 weeks and 3 days (SD 9 days), and the mean birth weight
was 3342 (SD 449) g.
We compared the demographic and clinical characteristics
between children born to people with high pregestational BMI and
those with normal-weight pregestational BMI (Table 1). As expected,
the groups differed significantly in mean pregestational BMI (mean

[SD], exposed, 30.4 [5.2] vs. unexposed, 22.0 [1.6]; p < 0.001). There
was also a trend toward a higher prevalence of lower income (<CAD
$40,000) among those born to people with high pregestational BMI.
Other demographic characteristics of pregnant individuals were similar among groups. Child characteristics, including birth weight, gestational age, sex, and age, at the time of scanning did not differ
significantly among groups.
Primary analysis
Children born to people with high pregestational BMI (≥25.0 kg/m2)
showed lower FA in the superior longitudinal fasciculus (B [SE]
= 0.82 [0.40]; p < 0.05), as well as in the body (B [SE] = 0.85
[0.39]; p < 0.05) and splenium of the corpus callosum (B [SE] = 1.29
[0.47]; p < 0.01), compared with children born to people with normalweight pregestational BMI (18.5–24.9 kg/m2
; Table 2; Figure 2). No
other significant differences in FA among groups were observed.

Secondary analysis
MD of white matter tracts
Children born to people with high pregestational BMI had higher MD
in the uncinate fasciculus (B [SE] = 1.31 [0.65]; p < 0.05) during early
childhood compared with children born to people with normal-weight
pregestational BMI. However, this finding did not remain significant
after correcting for multiple comparisons (Table 2).
FA differences for obesity and overweight groups
separately
No differences in FA of white matter tracts were observed between
children born to people with pregestational obesity (≥30.0 kg/m2
) and
those born to people with normal-weight pregestational BMI (18.5–
24.9 kg/m2
; Table 3).
Children born to people with pregestational overweight (25.0–
29.9 kg/m2

; n = 22) showed lower FA in the body of the corpus callosum (B [SE] = 1.68 [0.56]; p < 0.01) and the cingulum (B [SE]
= 1.48 [0.60]; p < 0.05) compared with children born to people with
normal-weight pregestational BMI (Table 3). There were trends
toward lower FA in the superior longitudinal fasciculus (B [SE]
= 0.84 [0.50]; p = 0.09) and the splenium of the corpus callosum (B
[SE] = 0.83 [0.48]; p = 0.08) compared with children born to people
with normal-weight pregestational BMI, but these associations did not
survive corrections for multiple comparisons.
In addition, no differences in FA of white matter tracts were
observed between children born to people with pregestational obesity
(≥30.0 kg/m2
) and those born to people with pregestational overweight (25.0–29.9 kg/m2
; Table 3).
Sensitivity analysis
The findings were similar to the primary analysis after excluding children born preterm, those exposed to diabetes during pregnancy, or
those exposed to alcohol during pregnancy, as well as after excluding
all three groups combined (Table S1). Moreover, removing gestational
age and birth weight as covariates from the model did not alter the
results (Table S2).
Subgroup analysis
In sex-specific analyses (male children: exposed, n = 18
vs. unexposed, n = 29; female children: exposed, n = 19
vs. unexposed, n = 24), significant differences in white matter tracts
were observed among groups (Figure 2; Table S3). Male children born
to people with high pregestational BMI had higher FA in the fornix (B
[SE] = 1.63 [0.74]; p < 0.05) compared with children born to people

with normal-weight pregestational BMI, although this association did
not survive corrections for multiple comparisons.
Whereas female children born to people with high pregestational
BMI had lower FA in the splenium (B [SE] = 2.21 [0.68]; p < 0.01)
and body (B [SE] = 2.55 [0.86]; p < 0.01) of the corpus callosum
compared with children born to people with normal-weight pregestational BMI, a trend toward lower FA in the fornix was also observed
among these female children (B [SE] = 1.63 [0.80]; p = 0.05). Importantly, the associations for the splenium and body of the corpus callosum remained significant after corrections for multiple comparisons.
Relationship with cognitive outcomes
Children included in the analysis did not differ significantly in baseline
or clinical characteristics compared from those excluded, except for
household income and age at the time of MRI scanning (Table S4;
Figure S1). The mean (SD) individual cognitive scores in children born
to people with high pregestational BMI and those with normal-weight
pregestational BMI are presented in Figure 3A and did not differ
among groups.
In the overall cohort, FA in the splenium of the corpus callosum
was significantly associated with WPPSI-IV VCI (β [SE] = 0.29 [0.12];
p = 0.02), whereas a trend was observed for the body of the corpus
callosum (β [SE] = 0.24 [0.13]; p = 0.06; Figure 3B–D). No significant
associations were found between WPPSI-IV indices and FA in other
corpus callosum regions or the superior longitudinal fasciculus
(Figure 3B).
When examining the direction of this association across subgroups, the relationship was stronger in children born to people with

high pregestational BMI, particularly in the splenium of the corpus callosum (β [SE] = 0.53 [0.20]; p = 0.02), whereas the body of the corpus
callosum showed a weaker, nonsignificant association (β [SE] = 0.26
[0.21]; p = 0.25). In the normal-weight BMI group, we observed
trends for positive associations in both the body (β [SE] = 0.26 [0.16];
p = 0.11) and splenium (β [SE] = 0.26 [0.16]; p = 0.12) of the corpus
callosum, although interaction terms were not significant (Figure S2).
DISCUSSION
The current study found that young children born to people with high
pregestational BMI exhibited lower FA in white matter microstructure
of the superior longitudinal fasciculus and corpus callosum compared
with those born to people with normal-weight BMI. The direction of
effect estimates was consistent across both pregestational obesity

and overweight categories. In addition, we observed sex-specific differences in white matter tracts associated with exposure to high
pregestational BMI.
Brain-behavior relationships were also observed in the overall
cohort, in which children with lower cognitive function tended to have
lower FA compared with those with better performance on a measure
of cognitive function. Overall, these findings suggest that exposure to
high pregestational BMI is associated with alterations in white matter

development during early childhood, with distinct effects on male and
female children.
Consistent with our initial hypotheses, children born to people
with high pregestational BMI had lower FA in the superior longitudinal
fasciculus, as well as in the body and splenium of the corpus callosum,
compared with those born to people with normal-weight BMI. This
study extends previous findings that reported differences in FA of
widespread white matter tracts, including the superior longitudinal
fasciculus and corpus callosum, in full-term neonates born to people
with pregestational obesity compared with those with normal-weight
BMI [13]. In addition, our findings are consistent with a previous study
showing a trend for lower FA in callosal fibers and the superior longitudinal fasciculus at age 6 years among children born to people with
high pregestational BMI [14]. A novel finding in the current study was
that lower FA in the aforementioned white matter tracts
was observed among children born to people with pregestational
overweight compared with those with normal-weight BMI, although
this did not survive multiple correction. Furthermore, we compared
FA in white matter tracts between children born to people with pregestational obesity and those with normal-weight BMI, as well as
between children born to people with pregestational obesity and
overweight, but found no significant differences. This was unexpected, as we anticipated lower FA in children born to people with
pregestational obesity compared with those with normal-weight BMI
or overweight, but the lack of significant differences may be due to
limited statistical power.
FA increases with age from early childhood to young adulthood in
typically developing individuals, presumably reflecting increased
coherence of axon orientation, increased density of axonal packing,
and greater myelination [24]. In this context, lower FA is often interpreted as indicative of lower coherence or density of white matter
tracts and/or poor myelination. Thus, our findings of lower FA in the
superior longitudinal fasciculus and corpus callosum in children born
to people with high pregestational BMI may suggest lower coherence
or density of these tracts.
To date, the precise mechanisms through which high pregestational BMI is linked to altered white matter development in offspring
remain unknown. However, some biological mechanisms have been

proposed. One such proposed mechanism involves proinflammatory
cytokines. In individuals with normal-weight pregnancies, most inflammatory cytokines in the maternal circulation increase over the gestational weeks [25]. In pregnancies complicated by obesity, elevated
expression of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin (IL)-6, IL1β, and C-reactive protein has been observed [26, 27]. Importantly,

studies have indicated that these elevated maternal cytokines levels
do not directly correlate with fetal cytokine levels, suggesting that
maternal cytokines may not cross the placenta into fetal circulation [28]. Instead, it has been proposed that these alterations in
maternal cytokines influence fetal development through placental
pathways related to inflammation, immune response, and oxidative
stress [29]. Furthermore, individuals with pregestational obesity often
exhibit altered metabolic factors, including hyperinsulinism, insulin
resistance, and changes in lipid profile. Given that the placenta serves
as a critical interface between maternal and fetal environments, it
likely plays a significant role in fetal programming and inflammatory
responses, particularly neuroinflammation, which could potentially
disrupt white matter development by disrupting glial cell proliferation,
thereby affecting the development of myelin sheaths around neuronal
axons postnatally.
The fetal brain is highly sensitive to environmental exposures [30],
which are thought to shape fetal brain development to meet the
demands of postnatal life [31]. In our study, we examined 11 major
white matter tracts and observed that children exposed to high pregestational BMI had lower FA in the superior longitudinal fasciculus
and corpus callosum compared with children born to people with normal-weight BMI. These tracts have been widely reported in studies
that have investigated the impact of prenatal environmental exposures on white matter development, such as exposure to endocrinedisrupting chemicals or ethanol [32, 33]. For example, Lebel et al.
reported significant differences in diffusion parameters of these tracts

between children with and without prenatal alcohol exposure [32]. In
general, white matter develops in a hierarchical order, with limbic
tracts and projection fibers (e.g., visual pathways) developing predominantly during the second trimester, followed by the commissural
tracts (i.e., corpus callosum), and, finally, the intrahemispheric association tracts (e.g., superior longitudinal fasciculus) [34]. If we assume
that prolonged exposure of white matter tracts to a disturbed intrauterine environment associated with high pregestational BMI might
lead to alterations, we would expect to see these changes in the
earlier-developing limbic tracts, as they form earlier and are exposed
for a longer duration. However, our findings do not support this
assumption. Instead of observing changes in these earlier-formed
regions, we found alterations in the superior longitudinal fasciculus
and corpus callosum. Therefore, we could only speculate that there
are specific vulnerable areas associated with exposure to high
pregestational BMI.
Earlier studies have observed sex-specific differences in offspring
related to exposure to high pregestational BMI [35], with predominant

effects on male offspring. These studies have suggested that female
offspring may experience some protection from adverse outcomes
owing to anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective properties of estrogen. However, our findings contradict the existing literature. We
found that male and female children had distinct patterns of white
matter involvement. Exposed female children had lower FA in the
body and splenium of the corpus callosum, consistent with the main
findings, whereas male children presented with the opposite direction
in the fornix (i.e., higher FA) compared with same-sex children born to
people with normal-weight pregestational BMI. Interestingly, similar
sex-dependent effects were observed in children with prenatal exposure to alcohol [36]. These differences may be attributed to the
effect of gonadal hormones. Gonadal hormone exposure is thought
to play a significant role in accelerating or promoting early white
matter myelination in male children during specific developmental
windows. However, this accelerated myelination may subsequently slow, potentially delaying the maturation of white matter
until later ages, e.g., adolescence. Our findings suggest that high
pregestational BMI may differentially affect developmental trajectories of white matter maturation in male and female children, with
these effects potentially varying depending on the developmental
stage of the offspring [36].
Furthermore, a positive association was identified between FA in
the body and splenium of the corpus callosum and cognitive outcomes
in the overall cohort, which is consistent with previous studies [37]. In
a subsequent analysis, we observed a stronger positive association
between FA in the splenium of the corpus callosum and WPPSI-IV
VCI among children born to people with high pregestational BMI. To
our knowledge, this study is the first to report an association between
altered white matter development and poor cognitive outcomes in
early childhood in relationship to exposure to high pregestational
BMI. As discussed earlier, high pregestational BMI is known to be
associated with chronic inflammation and disrupted metabolic hormones in utero, such as lipids. These disruptions may interfere with
critical periods of corpus callosum development, which, in turn, could
contribute to poorer cognitive outcomes.
Some limitations should be considered. First, pregestational BMI

was self-reported and might be prone to misclassification, as individuals with lower BMI may overreport their weight, whereas those with
higher BMI may underreport it. However, prior studies have suggested that individuals can accurately recall pregestational weight and
height many years after delivery [38]. Second, self-reported alcohol
and tobacco use during pregnancy is susceptible to recall and social
desirability bias, potentially leading to underreporting. Third, the pregnant individuals in the study were highly educated, were nonsmokers,
and had high household income, which may limit the generalizability
of the findings. Fourth, although we examined the dose–response
relationship between pregestational obesity or overweight and sexrelated effects on white matter tracts, our findings should be interpreted with caution owing to the smaller subset of children in certain
subgroups. Fifth, the association between high pregestational BMI
and offspring cognitive outcomes was not statistically significant in
this cohort, likely owing to the small sample size, which may have
limited our ability to detect subtle differences in cognitive scores.
Despite this, the study highlights potential differences in brain development as a possible explanation for cognitive variability, which warrants further investigation in larger cohorts. Sixth, as multiple
statistical comparisons were conducted in this study, there is a possibility that some findings may be due to chance. Finally, although we
controlled for important potential confounding variables, including
gestational age, birth weight, and socioeconomic status, we cannot
rule out the potential for residual confounding from unmeasured factors such as paternal BMI status, feeding status, diet, and lifestyle during pregnancy, as well as genetic factors.
Despite these limitations, the present findings of alterations in
the superior longitudinal fasciculus and corpus callosum have important clinical implications. The superior longitudinal fasciculus is a longmyelinated bundle of neurons that extends from the anterior region
to the posterior regions of the cortex, playing an important role in language processing, attention, and visuospatial tasks. Multiple studies
have also reported that alterations in this tract are observed in children with neurodevelopmental disorders such as autism spectrum disorder. On the other hand, the corpus callosum is the largest white

matter tract in the brain, crucial for integrating and transferring information between both cerebral hemispheres to process sensory,
motor, and high-level cognitive functions. It is also believed to play a
crucial role in behavioral deficits seen among neurodevelopmental disorders. There has been a lack of mechanistic studies evaluating the
extent to which alterations in white matter tracts explain the higher
rates of poorer academic achievement and neurodevelopmental disorders observed among children of mothers with obesity. Further studies should therefore evaluate the mediating role of altered white
matter tracts in the associations between high pregestational BMI and
child neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Overall, our findings suggest that exposure to high pregestational
BMI is associated with altered white matter microstructure in children
during early childhood, particularly in the callosal fibers and superior
longitudinal fasciculus, with the former being associated with poor
cognitive outcomes. Importantly, the direction of effect sizes was consistent across both pregestational obesity and overweight categories.
Our study further suggests distinct effects on female and male children. Given the rising global prevalence of obesity, it is crucial to raise
awareness and promote healthy lifestyles and weight management
among individuals of childbearing age. However, considering the limited evidence regarding dietary and lifestyle interventions in pregnant
individuals with high pregestational BMI, our findings highlight the
need for mechanistic studies. Such research could inform lifestyle or
dietary intervention trials aimed at optimizing brain and neurodevelopmental outcomes in offspring of mothers with high
pregestational BMI.O
